item.title: 40,000 Samsung workers stage largest protest, threaten strike
item.description: Tens of thousands of Samsung Electronics workers rallied on Thursday at the company's semiconductor complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea, demanding higher bonuses and threatening an extended strike that could disrupt global AI chip supplies.

item.title: U.S. seizes another Iranian tanker as Hormuz crisis deepens
item.description: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps seized two container ships in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, marking the first confirmed vessel seizures since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February and further choking off one of the world's most critical trade routes.

item.title: Microsoft offers first voluntary buyout in its 51-year history
item.description: Microsoft is offering voluntary retirement buyout packages to a portion of its U.S. workforce, marking the first such program in the company's 51-year history. The one-time initiative, disclosed in an internal memo on Thursday, represents a new approach for the tech giant as it continues reshaping its workforce amid a sweeping industry pivot toward artificial intelligence.

item.title: Meta to cut 8,000 jobs starting May 20, more layoffs planned for 2026
item.description:
Meta is preparing to lay off approximately 10% of its global workforce — close to 8,000 employees — beginning May 20, according to Reuters, in what the company views as the first wave of broader cuts planned throughout 2026.

Three sources familiar with the plans told Reuters that additional layoffs are expected in the second half of the year, though the timing and scope of those subsequent rounds have not been finalized. The pace of future cuts may depend in part on how the company's artificial intelligence capabilities evolve, the sources said.

item.title: Nuclear power surges worldwide as Chernobyl's 40th anniversary approaches
item.description: As the world prepares to mark the 40th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster on April 26, nuclear energy is experiencing a resurgence that would have seemed unthinkable in the decades following the catastrophic 1986 explosion. More than 400 nuclear reactors now operate across 31 countries, with roughly 70 more under construction, and a growing coalition of nations has pledged to triple nuclear capacity by 2050.

item.title: Trump says Israel-Lebanon ceasefire extended three weeks
item.description: President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that the ceasefire between Israel and Lebanon has been extended by three weeks, according to a post on Truth Social, just days before the truce was set to expire on April 26. The extension came as Israeli and Lebanese diplomats held a second round of rare direct talks in Washington.

item.title: INNIO completes first 3 MW hydrogen backup test for data centers
item.description: INNIO Group and the Net Zero Innovation Hub for Data Centers have completed what they describe as the world's first demonstration of 100% hydrogen-fueled backup power at the 3 MW scale, a milestone aimed at replacing diesel generators in mission-critical data center operations. The test, announced on Wednesday, was witnessed by technical experts from Microsoft, Google, and Data4.

item.title: Trump threatens UK with tariffs over digital services tax
item.description: President Donald Trump warned on Thursday that the United States could impose a "big tariff" on the United Kingdom if it does not eliminate its digital services tax on American tech companies, escalating a long-running dispute over levies that Washington considers discriminatory against US firms.

item.title: House panel advances bill cutting US UN funding by 78%
item.description:
The House Appropriations Subcommittee on National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs advanced a fiscal year 2027 spending bill on Wednesday that would dramatically reduce US funding for international organizations, slashing contributions by roughly 78% and effectively zeroing out US dues for the UN regular budget.

The bill, released on April 22 and marked up on April 23, allocates $310.2 million for Contributions to International Organizations — down from $1.39 billion enacted in fiscal year 2026. It provides $489.5 million for UN peacekeeping activities, a roughly 60% reduction from the $1.23 billion provided in the current fiscal year. The legislation eliminates the International Organizations and Programs account entirely, cutting all voluntary US contributions to agencies including UNICEF, the UN Development Programme, and UN Women.

item.title: Oil surges past $100 as Trump orders Navy to fire on Iranian boats
item.description:
Oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Thursday as President Donald Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to "shoot and kill" any Iranian boats laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz, deepening a standoff that has disrupted one of the world's most critical shipping lanes for nearly two months.

Brent crude climbed more than 3% during the session, while West Texas Intermediate also rose sharply, as investors weighed the prospect of prolonged supply disruptions in the Persian Gulf. Asian and European stock markets pulled back from recent highs, with MSCI's global equity index retreating from a record peak.

item.title: Scientists discover seismic 'stopping phase' in earthquakes
item.description: Researchers at Kyoto University have discovered a previously unrecognized seismic signal — a distinct "stopping phase" — that marks the moment large earthquakes cease rupturing along a fault. The finding, published Wednesday in the journal Science, could reshape how engineers and seismologists assess earthquake hazards near major fault lines.

item.title: Oil tops $106 as stalled Iran talks drag Asian markets lower
item.description: Markets across Asia declined on Friday as oil prices climbed and stalled U.S.-Iran peace negotiations kept investors on edge. The losses followed a pullback on Wall Street, where the S&P 500 fell 0.4% on Thursday, halting a weekslong rally that had carried it to all-time highs.

item.title: Oil nears $110 in fifth straight rally as Hormuz standoff intensifies
item.description:
Crude oil prices climbed for a fifth straight session on Friday, with both major benchmarks rising over 1 percent as the Strait of Hormuz remained effectively shut to commercial traffic and diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran showed little sign of progress.

Brent crude futures rose 1.17 percent while West Texas Intermediate gained 1.12 percent in early Asian trading, according to the Economic Times. The move extends a rally that accelerated on Thursday, when Brent surged over 3 percent to close above $105 per barrel.

item.title: Trump orders military to 'shoot and kill' Iranian boats in Hormuz standoff
item.description: The standoff between the United States and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz showed no signs of easing on Thursday, with President Donald Trump declaring "total control" of the critical waterway and ordering the military to "shoot and kill" Iranian small boats laying mines in the passage. The escalating confrontation has pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel and brought global energy trade through the strait — responsible for roughly 20% of the world's oil shipments — to a near halt.

item.title: Macron rejects US approach to Iran at EU summit
item.description:
French President Emmanuel Macron called for a swift return to stability in the Middle East and publicly rejected Washington's approach toward Iran, declaring that negotiations must be "systematic" and rooted in diplomacy rather than military pressure or economic coercion. Speaking on Thursday at the informal EU summit in Ayia Napa, Cyprus, Macron warned that the spillover from the US-Israel war on Iran is unsettling the global economy.

"It is in everyone's interest for stability to return as soon as possible and for the world's economies to be reassured," Macron said, according to Al Jazeera. He added: "Dialogue with Iran must be carried out in a systematic manner, not through targeted blockades or similar measures".

item.title: Hegseth says US naval blockade on Iran is 'going global'
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declared on Friday that the U.S. naval blockade on Iran is expanding beyond the Middle East, warning that no vessel can transit the Strait of Hormuz without American approval.

"Our blockade is growing and going global," Hegseth told reporters at the Pentagon, according to Reuters. "No one sails from the Strait of Hormuz to anywhere in the world without the permission of the United States Navy."

Hegseth, appearing alongside Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force General Dan Caine, said 34 ships had been turned around from the Strait of Hormuz since the blockade began on April 13. He added that Tehran still has a chance to make a "good deal" with Washington.

item.title: Study: 36% of land animal habitats face compounding climate extremes by 2085
item.description: More than a third of all land animal habitats could be exposed to multiple types of climate-driven extreme events — heatwaves, wildfires, droughts and floods — by 2085 if greenhouse gas emissions are not rapidly reduced, according to a study published Thursday in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

item.title: China picks 5 global partners for Mars sample-return mission
item.description:
The China National Space Administration on Friday revealed the five international collaboration projects selected for its Tianwen-3 Mars sample-return mission, marking a concrete step toward what could become humanity's first retrieval of material from the red planet.

The announcement came during the opening ceremony of the 11th Space Day of China in Chengdu, Sichuan Province. CNSA said it received 28 proposals after issuing a call for cooperation in April 2025 that offered 20 kilograms of payload capacity to international partners. The five winning projects were chosen based on scientific value, mission support, engineering feasibility, and technological maturity.

item.title: Iran claims seized cargo ship was carrying dialysis supplies, demands release
item.description:
Iran's mission to the United Nations on Thursday condemned the American seizure of the Iranian-flagged cargo vessel Touska, claiming the ship was carrying critical dialysis supplies and medical equipment when it was intercepted on April 19 in the Sea of Oman. The statement, posted on the social platform X, described the action as "a flagrant breach of international law" and demanded accountability and the immediate release of the vessel and its crew.

The Iranian Red Crescent Society backed Tehran's account, stating in a separate announcement that part of the Touska's cargo consisted of raw materials needed to produce consumable medical supplies for kidney dialysis patients. The supplies belonged to Saha Medical Equipment Company, a subsidiary of the Red Crescent, according to the organization. "Any disruption in the supply of these critical items could directly threaten the health and lives of patients in need of dialysis services," the Red Crescent warned.

item.title: China moves to block US investment in top AI startups
item.description: The United States and China took dueling steps this week to tighten controls on each other's access to artificial intelligence technology and capital, widening a tech rivalry that has become a defining feature of the bilateral relationship.
